1001: D is correct because Amazon SQS queues decouple the order collection and fulfillment tiers so orders persist safely in a queue even when instances are added or removed, guaranteeing no data loss from a scaling event. Polling the queues ensures instances pull work only when they have capacity. Scaling the Auto Scaling groups based on the number of messages in each queue (ApproximateNumberOfMessages) is the right metric because it measures the actual backlog of pending work for each stage, allowing each tier to scale independently during peak hours. CPU utilization or on-demand creation of new Auto Scaling groups does not reliably track queue depth or prevent data loss.
1002: D is correct because DynamoDB global tables provide automatic multi-Region active-active replication, delivering the continuously available and resilient architecture required. Deploying the tables in multiple AWS Regions lets the gaming application survive a Regional failure and serve users with low latency. Provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling is more cost-effective than on-demand mode for a steady and growing workload because you pay only for the throughput you actually need with scaling headroom. The options using manual replication or DynamoDB Streams add operational overhead, and single-Region designs do not meet the resilience requirement.
1003: B is correct because an Amazon S3 File Gateway presents cloud-backed NFS or SMB file storage to the on-premises rendering application while transparently storing the data in Amazon S3, which keeps storage costs low. The gateway caches frequently accessed data locally, providing the low-latency access the application needs to maintain performance. This is the standard, most cost-effective way to give an on-premises workload file-protocol access to S3. Mountpoint for Amazon S3 is designed for compute environments on AWS rather than on-premises servers, and the FSx options add significant cost and complexity.
1004: C is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses and the AWS global backbone network to route international customers' traffic to the API endpoint in us-east-1 over an optimized path, significantly reducing latency for TCP traffic. Global Accelerator is built exactly for improving performance of non-cacheable workloads hosted in a single Region and is far more cost-effective than dedicated connectivity for each customer data center. CloudFront caching would only help if the API responses were cacheable, and Direct Connect per customer would be prohibitively expensive. Site-to-Site VPN traffic still traverses the public internet and would not meaningfully improve response times.
1005: A is correct because API Gateway with an SQS queue creates a fully managed, serverless ingestion pipeline that scales automatically to handle thousands of survey submissions per hour while decoupling ingestion from processing. A Lambda function polling the SQS queue provides concurrent, elastic processing, and Amazon Comprehend is the correct AWS service for sentiment analysis on text. Storing results in a DynamoDB table with a TTL set 365 days in the future automatically expires records after 12 months with no manual cleanup. The EC2-based option adds operational overhead, and Rekognition and Lex are not text sentiment analysis services.
1006: C is correct because the AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance Systems Manager Automation document is designed to manage patching of instances registered behind a load balancer by deregistering or draining the instance from the target group before it is patched, resolving the errors caused by patching instances that are still serving traffic. D is correct because Systems Manager Maintenance Windows let the company schedule the patching and automatically remove the instances from service during the patch window, reliably enforcing the new security protocol. Together these approaches handle load balancer deregistration and automated scheduled patching, whereas leaving the existing document unchanged or switching target types does not address the failure.
1007: C is correct because AWS Glue is a fully serverless ETL service, so running one Glue job per customer requires far less operational effort than provisioning and managing EMR clusters. Attaching a security configuration that uses client-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (CSE-KMS) encrypts the data at the point of processing, satisfying the requirement that data be encrypted where it is processed before landing in S3. Using customer-specific KMS keys per Glue job meets the requirement for customer-specific encryption keys. SSE-S3 only encrypts at rest in S3 and does not protect data during processing, and EMR options carry heavy cluster management overhead.
1008: D is correct because packaging the application in an AMI and referencing it in a launch template lets an Auto Scaling group launch capacity automatically and seamlessly scale based on demand. Because the application is stateless, it can tolerate Spot interruptions, and configuring the launch template to use a Spot Fleet provides the lowest possible compute cost. Attaching an Application Load Balancer distributes traffic across the dynamically changing instances and prevents the 5xx errors caused by a single overloaded instance. Running only two fixed On-Demand instances or resizing a single instance does not provide seamless scaling and costs more.
1009: B is correct because an S3 Bucket Key for SSE-KMS lets Amazon S3 generate per-object data keys from a single KMS key at the bucket level, dramatically reducing the number of requests to AWS KMS while objects remain encrypted with KMS keys. This directly reduces the KMS request and encryption costs for the frequently accessed objects. Client-side encryption still requires KMS calls from the application, SSE-C is for customer-provided keys not stored in KMS, and SSE-S3 would require abandoning the existing KMS-based approach.
1010: B is correct because AWS Application Migration Service with the AWS Replication Agent installed on the VMs is the purpose-built lift-and-shift (rehost) service that continuously replicates on-premises VMs to AWS for a time-sensitive migration. C is correct because after the initial replication completes, launching test instances to perform acceptance tests validates that the migrated workloads behave correctly before cutover, reducing risk. D is correct because the final lift-and-shift step is to stop operations on the source VMs and launch the cutover instances in AWS, completing the migration. The other tools do not fit a VM rehost migration: SCT and DMS are for databases and App2Container is for containerizing applications.
1011: A is correct because a Cognito identity pool is the component that exchanges a successful user pool login for temporary, scoped AWS credentials, giving authenticated users secure access to store their documents in S3; the user pool alone only performs authentication and does not issue AWS credentials. C is correct because an S3 VPC endpoint in the application's VPC allows the private-subnet application to reach Amazon S3 securely without traffic traversing the internet. Together these steps provide identity-based, least-privilege access to S3 from a private subnet. NAT gateway and IP-address-based options are not identity-aware and do not provide secure user-level access to the bucket.
1012: D is correct because an EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy based on the SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessages metric scales the processing tier according to the actual backlog of queued orders, which directly measures the demand on the application. Since the queue fills up during peaks and peak times are variable and unpredictable, queue-depth-based scaling reacts to real pending work rather than a fixed schedule or a lagging proxy metric. Target tracking automatically adds instances when messages accumulate and removes them when the queue drains, keeping order processing timely. Caching with ElastiCache or CloudFront does not address a CPU-bound processing tier bottlenecked by queue backlog.
1013: A is correct because Scheduled Reserved Instances provide discounted capacity for predictable, recurring windows such as running only 12 hours every Sunday, and they run on non-interruptible capacity that meets the no-interruption requirement. Standard Reserved Instances provide the deepest discount for the steady-state instances that run constantly from Monday through Saturday. This combination matches each usage pattern to the cheapest appropriate purchasing option, whereas Spot Instances risk interruption during the Sunday runs and Convertible Reserved Instances cost more than Standard when no instance-family flexibility is needed.
1014: B is correct because AWS Batch is a fully managed service that automatically provisions and scales compute to run thousands of image processing jobs, so the company manages no underlying infrastructure. AWS Step Functions provides serverless orchestration that automates the multi-step workflow with built-in error handling and retries, eliminating manual tasks. Amazon S3 is the ideal scalable, low-cost store for the large generated files. The ECS option requires managing EC2 capacity, and EC2 or Lambda-based approaches either add infrastructure management or hit function size and timeout limits with large files.
1015: A is correct because an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket caches the website content at edge locations worldwide, dramatically improving download latency with minimal configuration. S3 Transfer Acceleration uses AWS edge locations and the AWS backbone to speed up uploads, addressing the reported upload latency with just a bucket-level setting. Both features require very little implementation effort and no architectural changes, unlike re-platforming to EC2 instances or building multi-Region buckets with replication rules. Global Accelerator cannot be attached directly to an S3 bucket and does not cache content.
1016: B is correct because an S3 gateway endpoint is free of charge and routes S3 traffic from the private subnet over the AWS private network without traversing the internet, satisfying the security policy. Enabling it requires only a route table update, which also makes it the most cost-effective choice. An S3 interface endpoint incurs hourly and per-GB charges, and routing through a NAT gateway sends traffic over public infrastructure while adding NAT processing costs. A bucket policy keyed to NAT gateway IP addresses does not keep the traffic off the internet.
1017: C is correct because creating separate Kubernetes service accounts and using IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) lets each set of EKS Pods obtain short-lived credentials scoped to exactly one IAM role. Attaching the DynamoDB policy to the UI service account and the S3 policy to the data services service account enforces that UI Pods can access only DynamoDB and data services Pods can access only S3, applying least privilege at the Pod level. Placing both policies on the EC2 instance profile would grant every Pod access to both services, IAM policies cannot be attached directly to Pods, and option D reverses the required service-to-resource mapping.
1018: C is correct because AD Connector proxies authentication to the existing on-premises Active Directory without replicating or hosting directory data in the cloud, keeping centralized identity management in the current system with the least operational overhead. Integrating AD Connector with AWS IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on across all accounts managed in AWS Organizations, and permission sets map AD groups to the specific AWS accounts and resources each team needs. This avoids the heavy overhead of IAM users per developer or running a managed AD with trust relationships. Amazon Cognito is designed for application end users, not for granting developers federated access to AWS accounts.
1019: B is correct because an API Gateway resource policy can explicitly deny access from any source IP address outside the company's trusted internal ranges, ensuring the published API is reachable only from the approved addresses. Resource policies are evaluated at the API Gateway level before requests reach the backend, providing a simple and effective control without any infrastructure changes. Private integration is for connecting API Gateway to private backends rather than restricting callers, API Gateway is a managed service whose security groups you cannot modify, and APIs cannot be deployed directly into a customer subnet for network ACL enforcement.
